data.title: LLMNR and NBT-NS Poisoning Leading to Credential Capture
data.summary:
Legacy broadcast name resolution protocols were enabled across the internal
network, allowing an attacker to impersonate requested hosts and capture
authentication material from users and systems.
data.description:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS)
were enabled on hosts within the internal network. When DNS resolution fails,
Windows falls back to these protocols and broadcasts the requested name to the
local segment.

Because these broadcasts are unauthenticated, any host on the segment may respond
claiming to be the requested resource. The victim then attempts to authenticate
to the attacker-controlled host, disclosing its NetNTLM challenge-response
material. This material can be cracked offline or relayed directly to other
systems where SMB signing is not enforced.
data.impact:
An attacker with access to the internal network could passively collect
authentication material from users and service accounts without interacting with
them directly. Weak passwords can be recovered offline within minutes, and the
captured material can be relayed to other hosts, providing an initial foothold
and a route to privilege escalation across the domain.
data.recommendation:
1. Disable LLMNR through Group Policy:
   Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client >
   "Turn off multicast name resolution" = Enabled

2. Disable NBT-NS on all network adapters, either via DHCP option 001 set to 0x2
   or through scripted registry configuration of NetbiosOptions.

3. Ensure DNS is correctly configured so that legitimate name resolution does not
   fail and fall back to broadcast protocols.

4. Enforce SMB and LDAP signing so that any material captured cannot be relayed
   (see the related finding).

5. Monitor for hosts responding to name resolution broadcasts, which is a
   reliable indicator of an active poisoning attack.
